newsitem.title: USA: Illinois House approves electric deregulation bill.
newsitem.headline: Illinois House approves electric deregulation bill.

text.p: The Illinois House of Representatives on Friday approved a far-reaching electric utility deregulation plan, a spokesman for House Minority Leader Lee Daniels said.
The deregulation plan supported by large Illinois utilities, consumer groups and unions passed 85-12 with another 20 representatives voting present and one excused, spokesman Brian Timpone said.
Rep. J. Philip Novak, Democrat of Kankakee, and Rep. Vincent Persico, Republican of Glen Ellyn, sponsored the bill, which will be forwarded to the Senate for consideration.

Supporters of the measure include Commonwealth Edison, a subsidiary of Unicom Corp ; Illinois Power Co, a subsidiary of Illinova Corp ; Central Illinois Public Service Corp ; the Citizens Utility Board; the Illinois Retail Merchants Association; and the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers.
"The House has acted very responsibly. It is a significant vote," Marjorie Benzkofer, a Commonwealth Edison spokewoman said. "The Senate would be negligent not to address the issue."
Central Illinois Light, a subsidiary of CILCORP, and the Illinois Manufacturer's Assocation are opposed.
A House fiscal analyst said the bill approved Friday provides for 10 percent residential rate cuts in 1998 for Commonwealth Edison and Illinois Power customers and 5 percent in October 2000.

The plan would cost Commonwealth Edison an estimated $1.6 billion over three years beginning in 1998, Benzkofer said. The utility participated in writing the deregulation bill and was excited by the House vote, she said.

Central Illinois Public Service, Central Illinois Light and other utilities with rates lower than the Midwest average would take five percent cuts in January 1998, with additional five percent cuts in October 2000 and October 2002 if their rates rise above the Midwest average, the analyst, Andrew Scott, said.

The bill phases in a program allowing residential customers to choose their suppliers beginning in the year 2000 and finishing in 2002. It also phases in choices for all commercial/industrial customers by 2000, with large industrial customers beginning in October 1999.

The plan also provides partial recovery for the cost of investments made during the regulatory environment that may not be recoverable under competition, referred to in the industry as "stranded costs." Those costs could include construction of nuclear power plants, depreciation of assets and other debts.

The bill also provides $76 million of state funding for low-income customers, $100 million for development of renewable energy resources over 10 years from customer surcharges and $30 million for energy-efficient projects over 10 years paid by the utilities.
